Theodore Dreier writes on September 3, 1933 to Edward Corsi, commissioner of immigration, to obtain the Alberses' visas; Corsi replies on September 5. The Alberses believed that the visas had been granted thanks to the intervention of Mrs. Abby Rockefeller, approached by Philip Johnson, whom they called their patron saint. Johnson, in 1970, says he remembers no intervention by Mrs. Rockefeller. letters dated 1933-09-03 and 1933-09-05; Johnson's letter to Duberman of 1970-07-20 Consequences: the Alberses arrive at Black Mountain in fall 1933

A music critic for the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, 25, trained at Yale, at the Concord Summer School of Music, and abroad, Evarts writes to Rice on learning of the college's opening. He is hired for music thanks to his gift for improvising at the piano and his limited use of written scores, a candor that appeals to Rice. letter of September 7, 1933
The New York Times heads its article announcing the founding of the college “Coeducation in A New College,” a sign of how notable the decision in favor of coeducation was. article on page 3
First meeting of the Board of Fellows, typed notes in Raleigh; special meetings on October 2 and November 6, 1933.

Albers writes from Berlin to his friends Ludwig and Maud Grote in Dessau; without revealing the American invitation, he describes his bleak prospects and his daily English lessons. A typed letter; giving up their apartment; English lessons every day; a wish to exhibit his work Consequences: Documents that Albers knew little English but was learning it even before arriving in the United States

Approached about the United States, knowing little English, Albers sets to work at once and writes to Dessau; yet he keeps quiet about the invitation that will change his life Atmosphere: Caution and hope under the pressure of emigration Stakes: The secret of the coming departure, kept even from close friends
The college opens: 21 students, 13 of whom left Rollins and 8 with no Rollins past. 13 ex-Rollins + 8 new = 21 students Consequences: Birth of Black Mountain College

An opening with minimal fanfare: no invocation, no procession; the only speech, the appointment of Nat French as “student moderator”; a debate on the college laundry rates; Georgia, in his capacity as rector, calls on the permanent caretaker of the Blue Ridge Assembly to explain the fire precautions — which Rice would later call the right and proper thing — and then the meeting adjourns. Consequences: The college is launched with a simplicity it would seldom find again

No invocation, no procession; Nat French appointed student moderator; a debate on the laundry rates; Georgia calls on the caretaker about fire precautions; the meeting adjourns, the college is launched. Words: Rice would later say that Georgia did the right and proper thing in calling on the caretaker Atmosphere: Simplicity, understatement, the sound of the mountains Stakes: The birth of a community that rejects academic rituals

Headline of the article announcing the opening: “Progressive Education Becomes Collegiate” — setting the tone for the comparisons with progressive education that Rice detested but could never banish from the press. headline, p. 3 Consequences: the “progressive” label stuck to the college despite Rice's protests
The college bylaws adopted; amended on May 2, 1934; meeting of December 8, 1934 on the role of students.

Adoption of the bylaws of the Black Mountain College corporation, providing in particular that the tenure of the founding teachers is to be determined by the Board of Fellows, with a guarantee for those already in post. without prejudice to the incumbents

At the end of November 1933, three New York newspapers announce on their front pages the arrival of the professor fleeing the Nazis, “A Tutor from the Bauhaus,” come to reorganize the art department of a mountain college. Words: “Liberalism Curbed in Germany,” Brooklyn Daily Eagle. Atmosphere: An echo of the German exile in the American press. Stakes: The Bauhaus lands in North Carolina.

Thanks to MoMA's public relations, the New York Times (November 29) and the New York Herald Tribune (December 10) announce the arrival of Albers, who came on the liner Europa; a revolution in American art teaching is predicted. Quotations: “the beginning of a new era here in the teaching of art” Consequences: Immediate renown for Albers and the college.
A typed letter to the Kandinskys (copies also to the Perdekamps and the Grotes), with handwritten notes added in each case; a comment on Duchamp added by hand.

A newspaper article detailing their past at the Bauhaus (its recent closing due to Hitler's policies), the role of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, Albers's “Material Technic” course — the only course required for all departments (theater, dance, music, art) —, his theory of all artistic creation as “form-giving,” his painting on glass, and Anni as a textile designer noted for her unusual materials, notably a synthetic material made of straw used for tapestries. It also mentions Hilda Ream (publicity and English) and John Evarts (music). The college described as the only one in the United States under the direct control of its faculty; textile materials made of straw.
The Asheville Citizen announces the arrival of Josef and Anni Albers at Black Mountain College (document kept at the JAAF). press clipping dated December 5, 1933

Ted and Bobby Dreier wait at the station with their rickety Model A convertible; a drive over back roads and dirt tracks to the campus; discovery of Robert E. Lee Hall and its columns; Anni goes up, touches one, finds wood under the fake stone; posters nailed to the columns. Words: Anni's interpretation: American things are not always what they seem (the first lesson). Atmosphere: dirt roads, a white Old South mansion, Anni's amused doubt Stakes: the Old World meets an America of facades — the beginning of the pedagogy of starting from zero

The couple pose in formal dress in a corner: he in jacket and tie, eyes averted, hands clasped; she in fur, cloche, and veil, looking toward the lens Words: Caption: “Germans to Teach Art Near Here” Atmosphere: The grain of the newspaper, the stiffness and anxiety of recent immigrants Stakes: The Bauhaus lands in rural Appalachia

The American Association of University Professors votes to strike Rollins from the list of voting members, the same day that the United States Naval Academy and Brenau College are declared ineligible. three institutions sanctioned on December 31, 1933 Consequences: opens the way for Rice's election as rector of the college for its second year, with Georgia as secretary

Albers describes his teaching experience at the Bauhaus in a letter to the president of Bennington; it is decided that Mrs. Leigh, on her way from Florida to Vermont, will stop at BMC in March to meet Albers. Consequences: A markedly less enthusiastic letter from Leigh follows on March 26

After Mrs. Leigh's visit, a lukewarm letter from Leigh; Albers, believing it to be a problem of English, replies in German, proposes a visit from April 8 to 15, and details his diplomas; Leigh refuses for good, citing the need for an American profile. Words: Leigh: they need someone of more essentially American experience who knows the “background of our girls”; the department already has a member of German background Atmosphere: Surface politeness, wounded pride Stakes: Albers a foreigner even in the modernist circles that invited him

President Leigh turns down Albers's candidacy, supported by Mrs. Swan (a former trustee and a parent), citing the need for a person with American experience: the department already has a member of German origin who speaks English poorly. Leigh's letter of April 6, 1934; the phrase: “German background and with very little understanding of the English language.” Consequences: Albers, who does not take the rejection lightly, consults Philip Johnson.
Johnson suggests that the German factor was only a pretext and that Albers might have a better chance at Bennington the following year. Johnson's letter of April 17, 1934.
A letter cited in a note, the first evidence of the correspondence between Albers and Perdekamp
The minutes of the student meeting of January 14, 1935 record that the students had collected $816 by that date (as part of a subscription connected with the Rollins troubles). $816

The article “Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?”: Rosen had pointed out to Einstein the oddities of entangled wave functions; Podolsky wrote the paper. This is the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) paradox. Physical Review 47 (10), pp. 777-780 Consequences: The notion of quantum entanglement, the basis of later work.
An untitled presentation, manuscript kept in the JA Papers.
An article in The Asheville Citizen: “Photographs of W.N.C. Scenery Prove Popular” (p. 24), showing that the enthusiasm for mountain photography went beyond BMC.
A postcard sent from Mexico with a photo of children in front of a large cactus, postmarked January 11, 1936, private collection in Germany. photo of children in front of a large cactus

After 400 km by car and three weeks of travel, Josef writes his old German friend a postcard decorated with children in front of a large cactus, summing up his impressions in brief notes. Words: “Indios (90 %), pirámides, palmeras cactos tropicales, loros, océano maravilloso. Clima estupendo, sol cegador y fresco porque altitud México de 2000 m […] El arte antiguo increíble.” Atmosphere: Blinding sun but the coolness of altitude; restrained enthusiasm. Stakes: The spark of a fascination that will transform all his work.

After three weeks on the road and 4000 km by car, Josef writes briefly to his old friend who stayed in Germany and mails a picture postcard of children in front of a large cactus, postmarked January 11, 1936. Words: Three weeks in a country of immense beauty: Indians (90%), pyramids, palm trees, cactus, tropics, parrots, an admirable ocean; a marvelous climate; the ancient art incredibly good. Atmosphere: Restrained enthusiasm, an overflow of impressions, dazzling sun. Stakes: The émigré from the Bauhaus discovers a new art that will be fundamental to his American painting.

Overnight, Evarts and Sly replace Steinau's Mondrian with a rectangular board covered in white striped oilcloth, of identical dimensions; the original is hung in another student's room. News of the disappearance spreads like wildfire; Albers, furious, declares that the painting is worth 50,000 dollars (Anni cuts that figure sharply). A student meeting is called and a search organized; within a few hours the pranksters, too frightened by Albers's anger, put the Mondrian back without ever confessing. A mostly white Mondrian with a red and yellow square; an oilcloth board of exactly the same size; declared value $50,000 Consequences: No damage to the painting; the culprits were never unmasked at the time

They find a striped white oilcloth board exactly the size of the Mondrian; after Steinau goes to bed, they slip into his room, take down the original, and hang it in another student's room. The next day, general panic: the Mondrian has disappeared. Albers nearly has kittens on the spot and cites a value of $50,000, which Anni lowers; a student meeting is called and a search launched; within a few hours the painting reappears in Steinau's room; the pranksters keep silent, Albers muttering “Ein sehr schlechter Witz !” Words: Albers: the painting is worth 50,000 dollars; “Ein sehr schlechter Witz !”; Evarts and Sly finding the praise of the painting far-fetched Atmosphere: A tiptoeing night, rumor spreading like wildfire, daytime panic, quick relief, fear of Albers's anger Stakes: A student prank against Albers's authority and taste; the line between reverence and irreverence toward modern art

John notes the natural/unnatural problem of physical attraction, dangerous and always to be kept in check, a conflict between the duty to control and the refusal to control, heightened by the close watch of community life.

One windy May morning, Alderman Manly Morison finds Viola, a little Black girl, throwing stones at the sheet-metal billboards while keeping a rhythm (1–1–1,2,3) and shouting “Eeeeee! Iiiii!” He interrupts her rhythm; she nearly bursts into tears, then asks what these fences were for. He remembers the advertisements and turns pale, dizzy before that old madness; tears roll down his cheeks. He laughs, imagining a billboard doing acrobatics; she joins in with a clear laugh, and he promises to have the fence torn down that very afternoon. stone, percussion written “Bang!”; flakes of glue and paper; the scene is dated the morning of May 9, 19— Consequences: decision to tear down the billboards

Manly and Viola go through the hedge: meadow flowers — white-lashed daisies, buttercups, fire-colored devil's paintbrush; a young linden (to be seen again further on, the narrator says); the wind has swept the clouds away, the sky a breathing blue, the grass nearly knee-high. Viola picks up an old milk bottle full of earth that gives a squeaky note; she says she plays the viola. old milk bottle full of earth; “it has a squeak note”

Around 4:30 p.m., about a hundred chairs; three billboards are to be torn down, the fourth, draped in a yellow curtain, will be kept. Meyer Leibow gives a speech: the advertisements rested on stimulus-response, and that was an insult; they shouted “Buy!” without courtesy, took a familiar tone, exploited babies and sex, sold a social status one notch above what was attainable, abused rhymes and the grammar of the absolute comparative, enlisted philosophy, science, and everyday language, and instilled a habit of lying. The elders, moved, shift in their chairs, tears in their eyes, for they had not always resisted. Meyer concludes that those advertisements did not survive; so the billboards are coming down. No applause: there was nothing in it to rejoice over. 4:30 p.m.; about a hundred chairs; yellow curtain; children playing ball a few hundred meters away Consequences: the three billboards are torn down

Viola strikes the billboards to the rhythm 1–1–1,2,3, shouting; the alderman says “Bang!” and breaks the rhythm; she nearly cries and asks what the tin panels were for; he turns pale and weeps as he remembers, then laughs at the idea of an acrobatic billboard; she joins in; he promises to tear the fence down that afternoon and speaks of a “program”; she is surprised that a program should be needed for so little Words: she tells him he broke the rhythm; she asks what the tin fences were for; “Program!” just to tear down a fence— Atmosphere: May wind, glue and paper raining down, tears and then shared, clear laughter Stakes: the passage from a despised world of advertising to a free community, seen through a child's eyes

Meyer lists the insults of advertising (stimulus-response, shouting, familiarity, babies, social status, rhymes, philosophy, the habit of lying); the elders shift in their seats, eyes brimming, for they had not always resisted; he concludes that those advertisements did not survive, so the billboards are coming down; he sits back down in the audience; no applause Words: “Stimulus! Response! Can you imagine such a belief?”; they did not survive; so today we are tearing down these billboards Atmosphere: grave attention, the gentle shame of the elders, the yellow curtain in the wind Stakes: a community lucidly mourns its own past naïveté
Albers presents a paper at the college's first general meeting (document “JA Papers”).
The minutes of two faculty meetings (September 28 and October 12, 1936) mention Albers, presumably regarding his teaching. Minutes preserved through the North Carolina Office of Archives and History.

Rice tells a philosophy professor, worried about his teaching, to his face that he should leave teaching and become a golf pro; three decades later he stands by it: that was what the man did best, and the colleague was furious faculty meeting of December 6, 1936, Minutes (BMCP, N.C. Archives) Consequences: A storm within the faculty

The professor confides to Rice his worry about his teaching; Rice looks him straight in the eye and tells him to leave teaching and become a golf pro; an uproar within the faculty; thirty years later Rice tells the story with a shrug, without apology Words: “You really should get out of teaching… you ought to be a golf pro”; later: “Well, I meant it. He was a wonderful teacher of golf” Atmosphere: head-on, brutal; then, in hindsight, a sulky, provocative innocence Stakes: Rice's double nature: wounding frankness and real insight into people

Speaking to visiting students, Rice explains that the college is not an ideal community but a place of education: people come to do what they have to do and then leave, hence the lack of emphasis on graduation.

On the eve of Josef's 49th birthday, Anni (37) writes in German to Ted, “Dearest”: if Weimar was her refuge from Berlin, Black Mountain is her refuge from Manhattan; she says she is at a loss, unable to be communist and Nazi at once. A busy day: breakfast with a “Miss Post”; at noon, cocktails at the home of the architect William Lescaze — she stands for an hour and a half amid the white plaster and curved glass, probably with only a glass of water, worn out physically (no arches in her feet, malformed legs) and socially; she thought herself terribly awkward. Joseph Hudnut (dean of Harvard's Graduate School of Design, who invited Gropius) and Lawrence Kocher (editor of Architectural Record, which the previous September had published an article on Black Mountain in an issue on the education of architects) are kind; Kocher will advocate Albers-Breuer-Gropius collaborations. A good conversation with Philip Youtz, director of the Brooklyn Museum, who is creating departments of textiles and industrial arts and invites her for the next day; a “Mrs. Swan” is not nice (Anni does not know who she is), while Mr. Swan is. At dawn, Anni had met the ship of Walter and Ise Gropius, who were coming to make America their new homeland — she whose life, at 22, had been changed by Gropius's few paragraphs on the Bauhaus. up before 6 a.m. for the Gropiuses' ship; 1 hour 30 minutes on her feet at the reception Consequences: Anni's role as a conduit of modernism to the United States
Letter preserved in the Albers-Dreier correspondence collection in the archives of the Josef & Anni Albers Foundation, cited in a note.

Anni on her feet for an hour and a half amid white walls and curved glass, probably with a glass of water in hand; conversations with Hudnut, Kocher, Youtz; inexplicable coldness from a Mrs. Swan she does not know Words: “I think I was terribly awkward” Atmosphere: icy elegance, physical fatigue, and unease Stakes: The outsider at the heart of New York modernism

Anni gets up before 6 a.m. to meet Walter and Ise, who are coming to make America their new homeland; no details of the meeting Atmosphere: dawn, a reversal of roles Stakes: The woman whose life Gropius changed at 22 welcomes him

April 7: the mighty Board sat with the four, and little came of it. April 8: it is decided that Fred and Mrs. Moellenhoff will talk to them; the problem is referred to the next day's student meeting. April 9: the student meeting discusses the college's opinion on trips by mixed groups; provisional agreement: mixed groups do not go on vacation together. Words: “The mighty Board sat today with the four. Little came out of the meeting” (Steinau's diary) Atmosphere: Administrative solemnity, hopes of clarity disappointed Stakes: How to sanction a fault that no rule named

At the last general meeting of the year, eight students announce that they are leaving. Their grievances: puritanical moral attitudes, an atmosphere of malicious gossip, limited student participation in decisions, Rice's brutality toward students, the rector's excessive power, low salaries used to push people out. Consequences: The discussion drifts toward faculty salaries

Moe writes that the longer he lives, the more convinced he is that the capacity for self-government is the exclusive heritage of the British, the Americans, and probably the Scandinavians; Rice has just had an illustration of why Cubans cannot govern themselves.

It was Rice who, as early as September 1937, first proposed the idea of summer institutes of music and art lasting four to five weeks; after general agreement, he asked the music and art teachers to plan the sessions and report to the full faculty. Session of 4 to 5 weeks Consequences: The summer institutes, associated with the Albers era, made the college's reputation.
Rice writes that the year is beginning very well, calmer than ever, and that he has relished the absences. Quotation: “I have fairly revelled in the enjoyment of absences”

Letter from Kocher to Theodore Dreier proposing that the design of the new Lake Eden campus be entrusted to Gropius and Breuer, recent German émigrés teaching at Harvard. Dated letter, preserved in the Dreier papers Consequences: The college commissions a Gropius-Breuer design, judged too complex and costly for the wartime economy
The Asheville Citizen reports an exhibition of the Alberses' designs in a Chicago shop (“Albers Designs on Display in Chicago Shop”). article in the Asheville Citizen, October 6, 1937

New York Sun article titled “Frau Albers Likes to Play with Warps and Woofs, and She Can Weave a Lovely Fabric Out of Straws,” a sign of the New York press's interest in her weaving. full title: “Frau Albers Likes to Play with Warps and Woofs, and She Can Weave a Lovely Fabric Out of Straws”
An example of the growing hostility between Albers and Rice after Rice's affair with Alice.

Mangold (secretary of the college) and Dreier (treasurer) meet Rice to set the terms of a leave: granted until May 1, but he may return only with the faculty's agreement; he will not solicit the students' opinion, and the students will be told only that Rice may or may not return before September. Leave until May 1; instructions regarding the students. Consequences: The rector is officially sidelined.

After weeks of “fearful stew,” private huddles, and formal meetings (without consulting the students), the faculty votes by broad consensus a leave for Rice until May 1, with a consultation procedure in mid-April through Mangold; it is decided that Alice will not be penalized. Words: Rice to Adamic: the college is in a state of “panic and almost lunacy.” Atmosphere: Fear, rumors spreading north, fund-raising threatened. Stakes: A velvet coup against the founder.

When Rice asks to cut his leave short, the Board of Fellows votes unanimously not to risk disturbing the calm and extends the leave until September. Furious, Rice refuses to represent the college at a meeting of progressive educators in Chicago and resigns as rector on April 13, 1938. Unanimous vote of the Board of Fellows. Consequences: Rice is no longer rector; Wunsch will later sum up the faculty's position.
Albers gives a speech at a college luncheon: life, not school, is the goal; the best proof lies in the results in later life
Photograph of a scene from Schawinsky's Danse Macabre, performed on May 14, 1938.

At the last Board of Fellows meeting of the year, Wunsch sums up: Rice had shown a lack of good judgment over time and dissipated his leadership and effectiveness; the faculty had in effect told him he was in no condition to lead; many had missed him — the stimulation of his conversation, his commonsense wisdom — and it was hoped that on his return in the fall he would again be the Rice of the college's early days.

Albers accuses Moholy-Nagy of having stolen the terms Struktur, Faktur, and Textur, published in 1928 in “Werklicher Formunterricht” and taken up in his Prague lecture, and of publishing them in Von Material zu Architektur (1929). On learning of a new edition of The New Vision, he demands the removal of the statements saying that he had continued Moholy's teaching at the Bauhaus. letters of August 28 and 31, 1938; Moholy will withdraw the offending passages Consequences: Moholy removes the remarks from the 1938 edition

On learning of the new edition of The New Vision, in which Moholy implies that Albers had continued his teaching at the Bauhaus, Albers writes a letter demanding the correction of “these two remarks… because they are not true”; three days later Moholy gives in and promises to remove them. Words: Albers: the remarks are not true; Moholy: their removal “meets with my own intentions.” Atmosphere: Cool epistolary courtesy between former colleagues. Stakes: Authorship of the Vorkurs; the pedagogical honor of an Albers already established in America.
A confidential memo to the Board of Fellows dated August 31, 1938, deals with his non-renewal; letters from Mangold (April 10 and August 31, 1938) attest to the antagonism toward him.
